questions.question: What are the advantages of adhesives? / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Adhesives provide uniform stress distribution, weight reduction, and the ability to join dissimilar
  • materials without damaging the substrates Even Stress Distribution: Unlike mechanical fasteners
  • (like screws, rivets, or bolts) that concentrate stress at specific points, adhesives spread loads evenly
  • across the entire bonded area, increasing structural integrity and fatigue resistance Bonding
  • Dissimilar Materials: They effectively join different or hard -to-bond materials (such as metal to
  • plastic, glass to wood, or carbon fibre to aluminium) without causing bimetallic or galvanic
  • corrosion. Weight Reduction & Thin Substrates: Adhesives eliminate the need for heavy brackets,
  • overlapping joints, or drilled holes, helping reduce weight in automotive, aerospace, and
  • manufacturing applications Preservation of Material Properties: Unlike welding or soldering,
  • adhesive bonding requires minimal or no high heat input, preventing thermal distortion, warping,
  • or changes to the metallurgical structure of the parts.
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: What are the advantages of synthetic rubber? / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Superior Temperature Resistance: Synthetic rubbers (such as EPDM and silicone) can withstand
  • extreme heat and severe cold without melting or becoming brittle. Chemical and Oil Resistance:
  • Many types—like Acrylonitrile Butadiene Rubber (NBR) —resist oils, fuels, solvents, acids, and
  • alkalis, making them ideal for industrial and automotive fluids. Weather and Ozone Durability:
  • Synthetic rubber resists degradation from sunlight, ultraviolet (UV) rays, oxy gen, and ozone,
  • making it long -lasting in outdoor environments (such as roofing materials and gaskets). High
  • Abrasion and Wear Resistance: It often provides greater toughness, strength, and resistance to
  • physical wear, tearing, and friction in heavy-stress applications like vehicle tires. Consistent Quality
  • and Supply: Because it is manufactured in controlled factory settings rather than harvested from
  • rubber trees, its properties and availability remain uniform and independent of agricultural or
  • seasonal disruptions. Electrical Insulation: Certain variants (such as butyl rubber) have low gas and
  • moisture permeability and strong electrical insulating properties. Customizability: Chemists can
  • engineer specific formulas (like Styrene -Butadiene Rubber or neopre ne) to match exact
  • performance needs for unique industrial uses.

questions.question: Briefly explain polymerization. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Polymerization is a chemical process where small, individual molecules called monomers bond
  • together to form large, high -molecular-weight chain or network molecules called polymers.
  • Addition Polymerization (Chain-Growth): Unsaturated monomers (often containing double bonds,
  • like ethene) link together rapidly without losing any extra atoms or producing byproducts.
  • Condensation Polymerization (Step-Growth): Two different functional monomers combine while
  • releasing small byproduct molecules —such as water (H₂O) or hydrogen chloride (HCl) —at each
  • step. Natural Polymers: Cellulose, starch, natural rubber, and proteins. Synthetic Polymers:
  • Polyvinyl chloride (PVC), polystyrene, nylon, and polyester.

questions.question: Recommend suitable finishing treatments for aluminium, brass and copper used in interior spaces, considering both durability and appearance. / [CO3] [5x6 = 30]
questions.solution_html:
• Finishing treatments for aluminium, brass, and copper depend on whether your goal is corrosion
  • protection, mechanical smoothing, or decorative coloring. Because these three metals behave
  • differently, they require specific finishing methods. Aluminium is lightweight and forms a natural
  • oxide layer, but it benefits greatly from engineered surface treatments for durabilityAn
  • electrochemical process that thic kens the natural oxide layer, improving wear resistance and
  • allowing the metal to be dyed in various colorsProvides a tough, colored polymer layer that seals
  • the metal against harsh environmentsUses abrasives or bead blasting to create a matte, satin, or
  • directional grain finish. A thin chemical film used mostly for corrosion resistance and as a primer
  • for pain. Brass (an alloy of copper and zinc) tarnishes easily in open air, so finishes focus on either
  • preserving its bright golden shine or giving it an aged/blackened look. Mechanical smoothing using
  • fine compounds and buffing pads to achieve a mirror shine, followed by a clear lacquer or wax to
  • prevent oxidation. Immersion in a potassium sulfide or specialized blackening solution to yield an
  • antique, dark bronze, or black patina. Acid dipping to remove scale and free iron from the surface,
  • restoring the bright base alloy. Copper is soft, highly conductive, and develops a natural green-blue
  • patina (verdigris) or brown tarnish over timeUsing chemical agents ( like liver of sulfur or specific
  • acid solutions) to artificially age copper into antique brown, black, or teal -green tones. Using
  • chemical agents (like liver of sulfur or specific acid solutions) to artificially age copper into antique
  • brown, black, or teal-green tones. Plating copper with nickel, chrome, or silver to improve surface
  • hardness and change its decorative appearance.
  • PART -C
